status_summary: As of 2026-10-13 DOE has acted on the reliability goals mainly through executive tools, and its main emergency-order tool lost a court test on 2026-09-11. Executive Order 14262 (signed 2025-04-08, published 2025-04-14) directed DOE to build a uniform reserve margin method, to use section 202(c) and other tools to keep generation critical to reliability available, and allowed it to block retirements of resources above 50 MW. DOE published its Resource Adequacy Report on 2025-07-07; DOE's modeling projects expected loss-of-load hours rising from about 8 to about 818 a year by 2030 if announced retirements proceed, and it recommends slowing retirements and adding firm dispatchable generation. POWER counted 43 section 202(c) orders and extensions since May 2025 as of 2026-04-02, holding about 4.4 GW of capacity open, mostly coal plus two oil and gas units at Eddystone; FERC accepted cost-recovery and cost-allocation filings tied to the Campbell and Eddystone orders in 2025. On 2026-09-11 a D.C. Circuit panel (opinion by Judge Pillard) in Michigan v. U.S. Department of Energy, No. 25-1159, vacated without remand DOE Order 202-25-3 of 2025-05-23 for the J.H. Campbell coal plant, holding that DOE exceeded its authority under section 202(c) by treating possible summer 2025 shortfalls as an emergency; the order had already expired, and petitions challenging extension orders are held in abeyance while challenges to orders for other plants are pending. On the FERC side, no rule requiring reliability pricing or backup procurement for the whole country was found, but on 2026-09-29 FERC accepted, subject to refund and a paper hearing, PJM's one-time Reliability Backstop Procurement of new capacity (effective 2027-02-28) and opened a section 206 proceeding under which it may later modify parts of the proposal; the procurement is open to storage, demand resources and other non-dispatchable resources, and FERC declined a request to give dispatchable generation further weight, so it is a partial parallel to the Mandate's pricing recommendation.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14262 directs DOE to publish a uniform reserve margin methodology, to use section 202(c) and other legal tools to keep resources critical to reliability available in at-risk regions, and allows DOE to block retirement or fuel switching of generation above 50 MW that would reduce accredited capacity.

DOE issues its Resource Adequacy Report under the order: it models about 818 loss-of-load hours per year by 2030 if announced retirements occur (about 8 today), assumes 104 GW of retirements, and recommends slowing retirements, adding firm dispatchable generation, updating adequacy metrics, and crediting generators by past performance.

POWER Magazine counts 43 DOE section 202(c) orders and extensions since May 2025, listing active orders that hold about 4.4 GW of coal capacity open (Campbell, Eddystone, Centralia, Schahfer, Craig and others) and pending challenges in the D.C. Circuit and the Ninth Circuit.

FERC's combined notice of filings lists a PJM proposal for an interim resource adequacy service and a large load registry; an earlier notice (2026-08-06) lists a PJM proposal for reliability backstop procurement. These are PJM filings under review, not FERC orders.

A D.C. Circuit panel (Chief Judge Srinivasan and Judges Pillard and Wilkins; argued 2026-05-15) in Michigan v. U.S. Department of Energy, No. 25-1159 (consolidated with Nos. 25-1160 and 25-1162), grants the petitions and vacates, without remand, DOE Order 202-25-3 of 2025-05-23 keeping the J.H. Campbell coal plant open. The court holds DOE exceeded its authority under Federal Power Act section 202(c), reads an emergency as an acute shortage not being timely addressed by states, utilities or grid operators, finds DOE's reliance on possible summer 2025 shortfalls and a five-year reliability risk insufficient, and notes the order had expired and that petitions against its four extensions (450 days in total) are held in abeyance.
timeline.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (opinion PDF as hosted by the Sierra Club)

timeline.event: Law-firm and wire reports of the decision: Willkie Farr & Gallagher says the court gave challengers a template against DOE's similar orders for at least six other coal plants and that DOE may seek en banc or Supreme Court review; the Associated Press reports a unanimous panel.

FERC accepts for filing PJM's one-time Reliability Backstop Procurement of new capacity (resources in service by 2032-06-01, a weighted-average price cap of 555 dollars per MW-day, commitments up to 15 years), suspends it five months to take effect 2027-02-28 subject to refund, sets a paper hearing on cost allocation, transmission owner exit and collateral rules, and opens a section 206 proceeding (EL26-108) under which it may later modify parts of the proposal. Eligible resources include storage and demand resources, and FERC declined a request to value dispatchable generation further (196 FERC 61,245; ER26-3380).
